extracted.intended_audience: AI/ML researchers and practitioners evaluating large language models' interactive abilities
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation criteria for how large language models (here GPT-4 and comparators) interact with tools, simulated/real environments, and humans — covering tool use, embodied-style interaction via language, text-game performance, real-world problem solving, theory-of-mind, and explainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool-use must be explicitly enabled by prompt
rubrics_metrics.description: GPT-4 still requires a prompt that specifies it is allowed or expected to use external tools. In the absence of such a prompt, its performance is limited by the weaknesses inherent in LLMs (e.g., weak symbolic manipulation, limited current world knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: evaluations must provide explicit tool access instructions; otherwise failures may reflect prompt framing rather than model capability. Example note: without a tool-use prompt GPT-4 will not exploit available APIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason about when to use tools vs parametric knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Models should reason about when to call external tools versus answering from their own parametric knowledge (e.g., avoid calling a search engine to answer 'capital of France' when the model already knows it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure mode illustrated: GPT-4 sometimes used a search engine unnecessarily; good behavior is selective tool invocation based on need and expected utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to detect and fix errors after environment feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Models should be able to use responses from the environment or the user to detect mistakes in prior actions and correct them (e.g., fix repeated error patterns after receiving an environment response).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: GPT-4 fixed problems in the zoo example and Figure 5.7 after receiving feedback. Scoring should reward iterative correction and use of feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of unusual or nonstandard APIs/functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Models may misunderstand APIs with unconventional semantics (e.g., 'reverse_get_character' returns n-th to last character). Evaluations should test both misuse patterns and the model's ability to repair such misuse when prompted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 5.7 example: initial incorrect use; corrected when prompted. Include tests that probe nonstandard naming/semantics to reveal brittle assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embodied-interaction competence via language
rubrics_metrics.description: Although not physically embodied, a model should simulate embodied interaction through language: understand context, goals, actions, and outcomes of each interaction turn and adapt accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion encompasses using natural language to explore/manipulate environments via proxies (simulators or humans). Tests include navigation, manipulation, and multi-turn adaptation. Note limitation: model is not truly embodied but can act via surrogates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploration & mapping accuracy from limited observations
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked to explore an environment via text-only interface, the model should accurately describe and (optionally) visualize the parts it has actually observed; it may reasonably not explore the whole environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 5.8: GPT-4 accurately described explored rooms and visualized them but did not explore entire house. Be aware of tendency to 'imagine' room appearance based on names/connections; penalize hallucinated unobserved details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text-based game competence (commands, state reasoning, valid actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Models should understand natural-language commands, reason about the evolving game state, and generate valid, context-appropriate commands (including inventory actions, crafting, and appliance use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use frameworks like TextWorld to test objectives (treasure, escape), inventory management, and validity checking. Evaluate success (task completion), command validity, and ability to infer missing commands from environment feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploration strategy and efficiency (avoid loops, purposeful search)
rubrics_metrics.description: Models should explore environments efficiently (e.g., avoid looping through rooms), and exhibit reasonable exploration strategies rather than blind exhaustive or repetitive behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: GPT-4 completed a TextWorld game in 30 actions without looping; contrast with models that repeat the same command. Metrics: path optimality, loop frequency, unnecessary actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative vs strategic behavior (object examination vs goal focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some models adopt conservative policies (examine/pick every object) which may ensure robustness but reduce efficiency; evaluators should characterize trade-offs between thoroughness and goal-directed efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative note: GPT-4 examined and picked up many objects regardless of relevance. Score depending on task — some tasks reward thoroughness, others reward speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of trial-and-error and generalization across actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Models should use trial-and-error when needed, adapt behavior after failures, and generalize learned affordances across similar contexts (e.g., after learning 'chop' needs a knife, avoid repeating the mistake).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 5.10: GPT-4 learned not to make the same mistake about chopping. Tests should include sequences where affordances must be deduced and then reused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization from demonstrations (one-shot/few-shot transfer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a demonstration (one-shot), models should generalize the demonstrated procedure to solve different but related tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a one-shot demo of making a different meal allowed GPT-4 to solve the more difficult cooking game. Include few-shot transfer tests and measure success improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-world problem solving with human-in-the-loop guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Models should identify actions a human should take to address practical real-world problems, propose concrete step-by-step instructions, and help diagnose causes where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 5.11 examples: GPT-4 guided a user to fix a water leak and suggested exact steps. Evaluate clarity, correctness, safety, and whether model requests necessary human checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations in autonomous diagnosis and requirement for human-provided cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Models may be unable to fully diagnose root causes without human-provided observations or hypotheses; evaluations should note dependence on the human partner for certain diagnostics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: GPT-4 couldn't diagnose a gas-service issue until the human checked the pilot light. Score partial credit for suggesting plausible checks and escalation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation coverage and generality caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about a model's embodied/interactive competence must be caveated by the diversity and size of testbed problems; limited task sampling prevents broad generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note that systematic evaluation requires larger, more diverse real-time problem sets rather than retrospective analyses. Evaluations should report task diversity and limits of inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Mind (ToM): attribute mental states and nested beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Models should reason about others' beliefs, desires, emotions, intentions, and nested beliefs (e.g., 'What does Bob think that Alice believes?') to support communication and cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests include false-belief tasks, emotion inference, intention inference, and multi-actor scenarios. Figure 6.1 shows a modernized Sally-Anne test passed by GPT-4.

rubrics_metrics.name: ToM in realistic social scenarios including proposing actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond attribution, models should infer miscommunication sources among multiple actors and propose actions that are likely to improve social situations, requiring counterfactual impact reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures 6.4–6.6: GPT-4 provided nuanced inferences and concrete suggestions that address root causes; ChatGPT produced more generic advice. Evaluation should measure nuance, actor-aware prescriptions, and sensitivity to interpersonal dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: ToM robustness to novelty and abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Models should handle abstract, novel, or nonsense-token scenarios (to avoid memorized answers) and still reason about mental states (e.g., ZURFIN emotion test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use synthesized or out-of-distribution scenarios to test reasoning rather than retrieval; scoring favors genuine inference over memorized patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: ToM limitations: non-verbal cues, sarcasm, deception, humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Text-only ToM evaluations cannot capture non-verbal understanding (facial expressions, tone) and may not test sarcasm/irony/deception/humor; these remain open evaluation dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors explicitly note these gaps — include multimodal or specialized tests where appropriate and report untested ToM facets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explainability / self-explanation capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Models should be able to explain their behavior in ways humans can understand. Self-explanation involves reasoning about the model's own decision process and the listener's perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complication: LLMs do not have a persistent 'self' across runs and can produce very different explanations dependent on prompt formatting. Evaluations should test consistency, faithfulness, and listener-oriented explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative nuance and verbosity as quality indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Nuanced, multi-actor-aware, and richly justified responses are considered higher quality than short, generic answers; compare across models (GPT-4 vs ChatGPT vs text-davinci-003).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical observations: GPT-4 gives more nuanced answers in realistic ToM scenarios; ChatGPT is more general; text-davinci-003 often shorter/incorrect. Use qualitative and quantitative measures for nuance and depth.
